c0006: Average number of events you work per year, counting every wedding, corporate event and private party. It is the main volume driver of the whole workbook: the P&L, break-even and scenarios all read it, and years 2 and 3 grow in events. Compare it with the capacity row further down (max events a year your bars and crews can handle).
c0008: Price per guest for a dry hire event (you supply the alcohol; we bring the bar, the bartenders and everything else), EXCL. sales tax and excl. alcohol: the bar package plus add-ons, with bartenders, mixers, garnishes, ice and cups included, the service charge in and the voluntary gratuity out. Price per guest incl. sales tax = this value × (1 + your sales tax rate). The example sits inside the per-guest pricing range in the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab; the Pricing Calculator builds your quote from your own costs and hours: divide its subtotal by the billable guests to bring it here.
c0010: Average number of guests per event across your whole mix, from private parties of about 60 to weddings of 120. Check Cherry booking data puts the typical event near 80 guests (see the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab). Sales per event = guests × price per guest. One cell for the whole workbook: the P&L, break-even and scenarios all read it, so they always agree.
c0012: Growth in events in year 2 over year 1 (enter 0.1 for 10%). Kept modest on purpose: two crews and a Saturday calendar cap how many events you can work, and weddings are booked about two months ahead, so referrals from venues and planners take a season to show up.
c0018: Share of BAR PACKAGES in total sales: bartending service, bar, mixers, garnishes, ice and cups. It is an INPUT: change it here and the P&L, the cash flow and the sales tax collected recalculate on their own.
c0020: Calculated as the remainder: bar packages + add-ons = 100%. Add-ons are travel fees, extra hours of service, glassware, champagne service and specialty bars.
c0022: Cost of goods sold on bar package sales: mixers, garnishes, ice and non-alcoholic drinks (Kit estimate; see the ice and mixers row in the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab). There is no alcohol in it: in dry hire the host buys it. Test it at a higher rate (more fresh juice, more garnish) before you trust the result.
c0024: Cost of goods sold on add-on sales: specialty bars, champagne service and rented extra glassware (Kit estimate). Set above the bar package rate because these items bring their own ingredients or rental fees. No alcohol: the host buys it.
c0026: Cups, straws, napkins, coasters and the printed drink menu sign, as a % of sales (Kit estimate). It sits next to cost of goods sold instead of hiding in miscellaneous. Some cities and venues restrict single-use plastics, so check the rules and price compostable cups if you need them.
c0028: Share of your sales booked through gig marketplaces such as GigSalad, The Bash and Thumbtack, rather than by hosts and planners who book you directly. Set it to 0 if you only sell direct. The marketplace sends you the booking and keeps a fee (next row).
c0030: Fee the marketplace keeps on those bookings. GigSalad charges 5% of the confirmed booking on its free plan and 2.5% on the paid plan, and nothing per lead (gigsalad.com); Thumbtack charges per lead instead, so convert that cost to a % of booked sales. Fees change: check the current schedule when you sign up. Not used while the marketplace share is 0%.
c0042: Monthly cost of the storage unit (or garage) where the bar, glassware and supplies live, plus the parking spot for the trailer. It is not storefront rent: you work at the host's venue. The deposit and the months before opening are calculated from this cell. If your county requires a commissary for ice or garnish, add it here (Kit estimate: +300-800 per month).
c0044: Months of deposit on the storage unit. Many facilities ask for about one month up front: far less than the deposit on a commercial lease. Agree it in writing.
c0046: Electricity and water for the storage unit (lights, the wash area, charging), plus any utilities the storage rent does not cover. Fuel for the tow vehicle and the generator is not here: it is in the "Vehicle and trailer fuel, maintenance and registration" line of the "3-Year P&L". It is the one cell for this cost, so you change it in one place and the rest of the workbook follows.
c0048: Yearly insurance: general liability plus liquor liability (Kit estimate 600-1,000), commercial auto covering the trailer (about 1,800), workers' comp for your W-2 bartenders (about 1,000) and equipment cover (about 300). Venues ask for a COI naming them as additional insured, and general liability plus liquor liability starts around 550 a year (insurancecanopy.com). The total is a Kit estimate: get quotes before you fix it.
c0050: Last-minute costs of each event: extra ice, mixers bought on the way, parking at the venue. It is a VARIABLE cost: it rises and falls with the number of events, so it cannot sit among the fixed costs or it would move the break-even without anyone noticing. Fuel, maintenance and registration of the tow vehicle and trailer have their own line in the P&L.
c0055: Principal requested from your lender: an SBA 7(a) loan through your bank, or a small SBA Microloan (up to 50,000). This is the cell. It is the only loan that the amortization schedule, the P&L interest and the DSCR use. The "Financing" tab checks that the sources of funds match the total cash needed on the "Startup Costs" tab (which includes working capital and the trailer and fit-out contingency): copy the loan suggested there into this cell until the difference reaches zero.
c0057: Nominal annual rate (not APR). The example (10%) is the kit's assumption for a small SBA loan. A smaller loan secured by a used trailer and bar equipment often prices above a storefront loan: ask two lenders for quotes, and ask about SBA-guaranteed loans, before you set it.
c0059: Total years, interest-only period included. A trailer and bar equipment lose value faster than a storefront build-out, so the term is shorter. SBA 7(a) allows up to 10 years for equipment and working capital.
c0079: The bar trailer, its conversion, the generator and the storage fit-out: everything that rides with the trailer is depreciated with it over the same life. Straight-line book depreciation; tax methods such as MACRS or Section 179 are separate, so confirm with your accountant.
c0081: Portable bar, bar tools, glassware, coolers, booking software and tablet. Loading and unloading at every event wears them faster than a fixed bar, so a short life is prudent. Straight-line book depreciation; MACRS or Section 179 are tax treatments: confirm with your accountant.
c0087: INFORMATION ONLY: it does not enter any calculation in this workbook. It is your estimate of the most events a year your bars and crews can handle: two setups (the trailer and the portable bar) times roughly 130 bookable days each, because Saturdays are the bottleneck. Compare it with the events per year you plan and with the optimistic scenario: if the plan goes above it, you need a third setup or more bartenders. Volume itself is driven by the "Events per year" cell above.
c0089: A new mobile bar does not book in month one what it books in month eight: weddings are reserved about two months ahead and the first year is slow (see the first-year row in the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab). Events per year above is the year-1 AVERAGE: the ramp only spreads year 1's sales across the months (slower start, stronger finish) and keeps the annual total. At 100% there is no ramp.
c0093: Converting the trailer, getting your permits and preselling at bridal shows takes weeks, so you pay storage rent and trailer parking before your first event. It belongs in startup costs, not in the P&L.
c0095: Calculated by formula on the trailer, conversion, generator, storage fit-out and inspection lines: if you change the trailer price, the contingency recalculates on its own. The note on that row of the "Startup Costs" tab lists exactly which lines are included.
c0098: Average days between the event and the money in your bank. A deposit (30% is typical) is paid when the host books and the balance before the event, so most of the money arrives before you work. Raise it if corporate clients or marketplaces pay later. The workbook does not model deposits: they improve your real cash flow.
c0106: ZERO by default: in dry hire the host buys the alcohol and your certified bartenders serve it, so you sell none. Selling alcohol requires a liquor license (and, in many states, a special event permit): see the full-service option in section 9 of the Word plan and check your state before adding it. Keep liquor liability coverage whenever your bartenders pour at an event.
c0144: A used bar trailer (6 x 12 ft cargo, concession or horse trailer) that you convert. The tow vehicle is yours, so it costs 0 in the plan: if you do not have one, a used pickup is an extra purchase starting around 10,000 (checkcherry.com). Prices vary a lot with size and condition, so get several quotes.
c0147: Bar top, cabinets, hand sink and fresh and gray water tanks, LED lighting and the electrical work. A basic conversion typically starts around 5,000 and a custom build costs several times more (Kit estimate).
c0149: Trailer wrap, signage and the bar facade: your rolling billboard at every venue and the first thing guests photograph.
c0151: A portable bar for the second crew and for indoor venues where the trailer does not fit. Basic units start around 1,000 (checkcherry.com); a nicer one with a lit back bar costs more.
c0153: A quiet inverter generator and the cabling, for venues without power. Typical range 800-3,000 (Kit estimate).
c0155: Shelving, glassware racks and a wash area inside the storage unit. Ask the facility what it already provides before you budget this line.
c0160: Business license, sales tax permit and responsible-service certifications (TABC in Texas, RBS in California, TIPS or ServSafe Alcohol) for year 1. It varies a lot by state and city: get the amounts for yours before you close the budget.
c0162: Only if your county requires it: ask your county health department whether ice, cut garnish or the hand sink trigger a unit inspection. If not, enter 0.
c0164: Booking software and CRM for proposals, contracts and deposits, plus a card reader and a tablet.
c0166: Shakers, jiggers, speed rails, strainers, ice scoops and bar mats for 4 stations: the equipment that gets depreciated. Daily disposables are NOT depreciated: they go in the disposables line of the P&L, at the % of sales set in "0. Assumptions".
c0168: Mixers, syrups, garnishes, cups and napkins for your first events. No alcohol: in dry hire the host buys it. With 0% recoverable input tax (the US default), any sales tax you pay on this purchase is treated as a cost.
c0170: Website, photos of the trailer set up, listings on The Knot, WeddingWire, Zola and GigSalad, Google Business Profile and your first bridal show.
c0172: Glassware (300 pieces plus racks), coolers, ice bins and dispensers for events where the host does not rent glass.
c0180: What you buy: trailer, conversion, equipment, launch and formation costs. The cash cushion is not an investment: it is working capital.
c0205: Bar package sales: bartending service, bar, mixers, garnishes, ice and cups per guest, for weddings, corporate events and private parties. No alcohol: the host buys it. All of it carries cost of goods sold at the bar package rate.
c0207: Add-on sales: travel fees, extra hours of service, glassware, champagne service and specialty bars. They carry cost of goods sold at the add-on rate.
c0213: Applied to the sales of THAT CHANNEL. With 0% marketplace sales in "0. Assumptions", this line is zero.
c0221: The monthly amount is typed in "0. Assumptions"; here it is multiplied by twelve. It covers your storage unit and the parking spot for the trailer, not storefront rent. The months before opening are on the "Startup Costs" tab and are NOT counted twice.
c0225: Electricity and water for the storage unit, plus any utilities the storage rent does not cover. Fuel for the tow vehicle and the generator is in the vehicle and trailer line.
c0235: Business mobile plan and data for the card reader at venues with weak signal. Get a quote from your carrier.
c0237: Replacing broken or lost glassware and repairing equipment. Glass breaks at events, so restock every season.
c0239: Responsible-service certifications for you and your bartenders (TIPS, TABC, RBS or ServSafe Alcohol) and their renewals. The certificate you need varies by state, and many venues ask for it anyway.
c0241: Tastings and drink menu consultations for couples and planners: mixers, garnish and your time. Many operators credit the tasting toward the booking: if you do, lower this line.
c0265: Floor set by this workbook: kit benchmark (editable estimate). The workbook's gross margin also subtracts card fees, marketplace fees and miscellaneous event costs, so it sits below the margin of bar package pricing alone.
c0268: Ceiling for cost of goods sold on bar packages and add-ons (disposables have their own line): kit benchmark (editable estimate). No alcohol in it: in dry hire the host buys it.
c0270: Ceiling for labor: kit benchmark (editable estimate). It includes your own pay as Owner & Lead Bartender plus the W-2 event bartenders and barbacks.
c0272: There is no storefront rent in this workbook: 6% is a prudent ceiling for the storage unit and trailer parking, a kit benchmark (editable estimate). A bar with its own premises carries a much higher occupancy cost.
c0274: Floor of 5%: a kit benchmark (editable estimate). A new business with a loan to repay starts lower: if you land under it, review the price per guest and the events per year first.
c0324: The SAME staffing in all three scenarios. In the pessimistic case your real cost of event bartenders and barbacks falls with the number of events (you pay hours per event), so the real result would be somewhat better than shown. If labor cost still blows up, adjust it in the "Staffing" tab, not here.
c0344: Sells, runs the tastings, designs the drink menus and leads the bar for crew 1. Covers the main shift at every event.
c0346: Leads the second crew on peak-season Saturdays: setup, service and breakdown. Part-time W-2, paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE.
c0348: Bartenders hired per event and paid hourly as W-2 employees. Their FTE is a fraction because they only work event hours. Voluntary tips are theirs (FLSA). Treating them as 1099 contractors is a misclassification risk (FLSA; California AB5). Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE.
c0350: Barbacks hired by the hour as W-2 employees: loading, ice, setup and breakdown at larger events. Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE.
c0379: 1. "0. Assumptions" is the control sheet: events per year, price per guest excl. sales tax, guests per event, the bar package and add-on mix, cost of goods sold, storage and trailer parking, financing and taxes.
c0382: 4. All figures are EXCL. SALES TAX. To turn a quoted price into a price excl. sales tax, divide it by 1 + your sales tax rate (with an 8% rate, divide by 1.08); if an item is taxed at a different rate in your state, use that rate. Sales tax on services varies by state: in some, the whole bar package invoice is taxable, including bartender labor and rentals; check yours. The rate of each sales line is in the "Sales tax rate on the line (%)" column of the P&L, and from it come the receipts, the sales tax collected and the equivalent price per guest incl. sales tax. With the default 0% recoverable input tax, the sales tax you pay on purchases and startup costs is treated as a cost; in the UK, enter 20% if you are VAT-registered.
c0421: A monthly storage and trailer parking cost, plus a deposit and rent for the months before opening
c0422: A mobile bar has no premises, but the bar, the glassware and the trailer have to live somewhere between events. Leaving it out makes the business look like it has no occupancy cost.
c0429: Two useful lives: the bar trailer with its conversion, generator and storage fit-out, and the portable bar with the tools and glassware. The Startup Costs tab calculates the annual charge.
c0430: The trailer and the bar equipment wear out at different speeds. Working capital, opening inventory and launch marketing are not fixed assets, so they are not depreciated.
c0441: A percentage calculated on the trailer, conversion, generator, storage fit-out and inspection lines
c0442: If you change the trailer price, the contingency recalculates instead of staying at the old amount.
c0462: Fuel rises and falls with the number of events you work: putting it among the fixed costs distorts the break-even.
c0465: Every bar package and add-on sale carries its own cost of goods sold rate, whatever the type of event
c0476: Price per event (median; excl. alcohol and tips)
c0479: 1,334 bookings since January 2024. Compare it with your price per guest × guests per event in "0. Assumptions".
c0483: The typical event runs about 80 guests.
c0487: Longer events cost more but less per hour: use it to set your extra-hour rate.
c0489: $375 for about 4 h, or about $75-$120 per bartender hour
c0491: The floor of dry hire pricing: a quick check for your hourly rate.
c0493: Deposit about 30%; 26% of bookings charge a travel fee (median 36 miles; free up to about 25)
c0495: Set your travel fee as an add-on, and ask for the deposit to secure the date.
c0497: October about 13% and May 12.4% of bookings; January 3.8%; median lead time 62 days; 85% Friday to Sunday
c0499: Peak wedding season (May-June, September-October) is where the Saturday bottleneck of your two crews shows. Shape the ramp in "12-Month Cash Flow" around it.
c0500: First year in business (12+ months of activity)
c0501: Median 3 events and $1,650; top 10% about 39 events and $35,500
c0503: The kit example is a fully built operation with two crews. The ramp in "0. Assumptions" and the pessimistic scenario show what a slower start does to your cash.
c0505: 2 in the first hour, then 1 per hour
c0507: Use it to size mixers, ice and cups, and to check how many guests one bartender can serve.
c0509: 1 per 50 guests (full bar); 1 per 75 (beer and wine)
c0511: Drives the people per event in "Staffing". Add a barback for larger setups.
c0515: BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, code 35-3011. Compare with the hourly rate in "Staffing" and with your state minimum wage.
c0517: GigSalad 5% (free plan) or 2.5% (paid plan) of the confirmed booking; nothing per lead
c0519: Thumbtack charges per lead instead. Fees change: check before you sign up.
c0521: Portable bar from about $1,000; tools $500-$1,500; lean start $2,000-$7,000; a converted trailer often costs tens of thousands
c0523: Compare with "Startup Costs": the kit example is a trailer-based build, not the lean start.
c0525: General liability plus liquor liability from $550 per year; from $275 per event
c0527: Venues ask for a COI naming them as additional insured: confirm what each venue requires before you buy.
c0529: Ice 1.5 lb (0.68 kg) per guest; mixers, garnish and ice about $2.25 per guest
c0531: Use it to check the cost of goods sold rate on bar packages. The real figure depends on your drink menu.
c0597: The same calculation on what you BUY (trailer, conversion, equipment, launch and formation costs), without working capital: that money is not spent, it is tied up and comes back when you close the business. Informational: the payback that is published is the one above.
